column2: Wunsch writes to Northwestern, Chicago, Swarthmore (John Nason), Johns Hopkins, Antioch, the U. of North Carolina (Frank Graham), Bard (C. H. Gray), Stanford, and Reed (Arthur Scott) about accreditation. Letter of May 7, 1942; replies between May 1 and July 9, 1942

Promised for August 1941, the manuscript is delivered in May 1942, with an added chapter on Black Mountain that had not been planned, at Canfield's request (he is known for Black Mountain, and the experiment is of exceptional importance). Nine months behind the promised deadline.
Letters to Mangold: Frederic Cohen (July 20, 1942), Carleton Sprague Smith (August 7), John Martin (August 8), Martha Graham (August 13) — recommendations concerning Bentley.

His book finished and his advance spent, Rice settles with his new wife in his mother-in-law's cottage; shortly afterward the son of this second marriage is born. Consequences: A new family and a new career as a writer.

The chapter “Rollins Was Holt” angers Holt, still president of Rollins College; he and Edwin Grover contact Harper and Brothers to contest malicious lies. The lawyers have already had the word “sycophancy” removed from among Holt's attributes. Rice stands firm and writes to his publishers that this is a sort of commando raid by General Hammie. The portrait of Holt: guided in turn by ambition, sentimentality, charity, Yankee cunning, pride, humility, and childlike wonder, with ambition always close at hand. Consequences: The book is withdrawn from circulation.

Betty Brett's diary (November 2, 4, 25, 1941), the faculty meeting of October 28, 1942, an open letter signed by the student officers, the students' decision to abandon the “bedroom” agreement, signed by William McLaughlin.

Time (in its “Brilliant Critic” column of November 23, 1942) hails his discourse on American education; Orville Prescott in the New York Times (November 4, 1942) describes him as two people in one body. Prescott: “sputtering chain of epigrams”; Time: Rice “has turned state's evidence against his profession”. Consequences: The book sets off on a successful course.

Faced with fears of libel, Rice holds firm and writes to his editor that the challenge is a sort of commando raid by General Hammie. Words: “I suspect that this is a sort of commando raid on the part of general Hammie”. Atmosphere: Cheeky defiance, wartime humor. Stakes: Rice sacrifices his literary success to his freedom of speech.

From late 1942 or early 1943, she traces the numbers on aircraft dials with a pantograph: right hand to trace, left for the knob, pressure with the foot, exactly like Charlie Chaplin in Modern Times; after the midnight shift, everyone goes bowling; a little radio beside her tuned to WQXR; she reads all of Swann's Way during the year Consequences: One of only two adult years without a brush; afterward she says she was in a totally different place

From 9 p.m. on, the artists settled at the tables pushed against the wall, facing the windows; one evening Kaldis proposes to rebuild the neighborhood with Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian colonnades; Elaine advises him to leave Eighth Street alone, a plain American market Consequences: the management ends up imposing restrictions: four people per table, no smoking, restrooms locked
Albers organizes an exhibition of Charlot's work at the college later in 1943.
In 1943, few people know about the college; Goulet learns of it purely by chance, by reading Louis [Adamic — text cut off]. Consequences: She becomes a student there in 1943-44

In 1943, few people have heard of the college; reading Louis Adamic's My America, won over by his description of BMC, she writes to the college for a brochure and immediately decides to go. a book, a letter, a brochure Consequences: she enrolls for the 1943-44 year

Begins in sociology under Dr. Miller; after a few months switches to art under Josef Albers. With no sculpture courses available, she goes into drawing and painting, despite training in ceramics since the age of eight. ceramics since the age of eight Consequences: her whole life oriented toward sculpture

Eight cows missing from the upper pasture. Departure at 6:00 a.m., a steep climb through thickets of mountain laurel, cool, misty air. Lake Eden and the valley drowned in a river of white fog slowly lifting. Three descents and climbs out of wooded ravines; by noon the witness, exhausted, thinks his lungs will burst. Dreier bounds over the rocks as if on rubber balls and finds all the cows by midafternoon; a descent at a run down the stony creek bed, Dreier flying ahead like water skipping over the rocks. eight cows; departure at 6:00 a.m.; mountain laurel; a descent at a run down the creek bed Consequences: the witness keeps from this speed an unforgettable knowledge and joy

Frantic anthill activity for days. Long ladders in the dining hall for the decorating committee; Albers clicks his tongue as he gives his directions. The English department rehearses skits: a sacred piece by Heinrich Schütz recently conducted by Jalowetz is turned into a musical revue about life at BMC — “God pity me a sinner” becomes “Pity me at dinner” (a complaint about the food). Eric Bentley, pink beneath his gleaming glasses, sings with the expression of a cantor opposite Professor Straus's Pharisee bass. Fritz Cohen adds compositions and a satirical libretto touching the community's most vulnerable points. Molly, deadpan, dances her Martha Graham solo, the Death of the Fly. Elsa Cohen and her dancers rehearse a wild cancan. Liese Kulka sings by herself the duet of the Count and Susanna from The Marriage of Figaro, alternating tenor and soprano, her back turned, black sleeves wrapped around her waist. Sam Brown plays boogie-woogie on the distant piano, young Swackhammer is on drums. Tables in a horseshoe, dances between courses before the silver curtains are drawn; a festive candlelit meal: turkey, trimmings, even asparagus. Frantic borrowing of belts and necklaces in the dormitories; a transformation from work jeans to black-velvet elegance in front of the North Lodge fire, wine and aperitifs. turkey, asparagus, silver curtains, black velvet, wine, candles, ladders

Students work in the mica mine with two local miners, who often disappear deep into the tunnels with their harmonicas and their jug of liquor. The mica, intended according to Roberts for gunsights and weaponry, served the patriotic war effort. Icy water up to midcalf at the bottom of the shaft; buckets of spoil hauled up by a rope winch worked by someone above; wheelbarrows pushed along a track of loose planks that often missed their destination; mica extracted in veins, large pieces cut out with a chisel Consequences: Work stopped abruptly when the main gallery collapsed one morning; the mine was never reopened, according to Roberts.
The pieces of mica were brought to the bindery in the Studies Building, where they were split into slices of a given thickness and then trimmed to government specifications.

Roberts recalls the periodic exoduses of a large part of the student body when a teacher, irreconcilable with his colleagues' position, left the college with his followers — Eric Bentley cited as an example. At one point in 1943, there were as many faculty members as students.
Elaine marries Willem de Kooning in 1943; he will teach painting at BMC in the summer of 1948; she dies in 1989 after a career as an artist, teacher, and writer. Summer 1948 at BMC

Faced with a profusion of vegetables, Molly Gregory tries to sell them in the village — she was nearly arrested — then at the Asheville market, where she gets a few cents for them. Nearly arrested in the village; “pennies” obtained in Asheville

After prolonged digging, the next stage requires dynamiting; too dangerous and without a permit from the state, the project is abandoned. The state refuses a permit for dynamiting Consequences: Hopes of millions from mica fall away

In his welcoming address at the start of the fall 1943 term, Wunsch declares that at the beginning of its eleventh year the college is in reality starting over as a new college, that the institution must take an organic form suited to the needs of those who make it up, that Black Mountain is first a community and then a college, and that a good member is one who builds good relations with everyone. The college's eleventh year Consequences: Some suspect the sincerity of his democratic rhetoric

The faculty decides that for outside purposes (transfers) evaluation will follow the generally accepted outside standards: no more formal grading; the student officers must take on the problem of absences; discussions of additional examinations; accelerated passage of students into the senior division for early specialization and a tangible goal. Consequences: “Codification” as the general tone of the war years; marking time, according to the historian

In private letters to John Evarts, Wunsch reports seeing Danny Deaver and Mimi French agree to go together to a Saturday night dance — he did not like the implications; on New Year's Eve, in the South Lodge lobby, he is deeply upset: too much wine has changed the little boys and girls into embracing “Greenwich Villagers”; he does not stay long. A Saturday night dance; a New Year's Eve party with wine

The student body refuses to adopt the traditional “agreement” forbidding visits to the rooms of the opposite sex except in case of illness; recurring agitation for an equal voice at general meetings and for moral standards to be open to discussion there. Consequences: Mild friction between students and faculty

Graveled paths lined with galax and laurel are laid out and the road banks graded; Albers works for months with a crew paneling and painting the dining hall and the lodge halls. Galax and laurel; paneling and painting Consequences: The site moves beyond its pioneering days

Dances after dinner, theater rehearsals, Saturday concerts often attended by wounded veterans from the nearby Moore General Hospital; Wunsch writes to Stephen Forbes that the good things go on. Wounded veterans from the Moore General Hospital

With the move to Lake Eden, the makeup of the faculty has changed radically; some newcomers, energetic and strong-willed personalities, want to make their mark and clash with established ways; but Albers, Dreier, and Wunsch still dominate — the absence of a power vacuum is in itself both irritating and stimulating. Consequences: Conflicts of personality and of community policy in the making
Joins the faculty in the fall of 1943 Consequences: Her fight for integration sets off the crisis

Early 1943: a program with faculty lectures on Black life and literature, a showing of the Harmon Foundation film on Hampton Institute, and a guest lecture by W. A. Robinson, director of the Negro Secondary School Study, on the Negro in the present world crisis and his hopes for the postwar period Wunsch cordially invites Black high-school teachers from Asheville: they should be sure they will be very, very welcome.

Summer 1943: Straus accuses Bentley at a faculty meeting of indoctrinating his students with a pro-Soviet and anti-British bias. Bentley defends himself with a seven-point statement. Bentley declares: (1) he is not a communist (2) he presents theories as such (3) he belongs to no political or religious group (4) his sympathy goes more to Russia than to the United States (5) he left England because he did not like the regime (6) his allegiance to Russia does not mean agreement with everything they do (7) his students can and do disagree with him; he writes for The Nation Consequences: The beginning of the political accusations that will feed the split
From 1943 on, intermittent tours: Cage plays his music, Cunningham dances. Consequences: In the spring of 1948, a new letter from Cage to the college.
In 1943, layoffs become necessary because of the war (letter from Dreier to Stephen Forbes, March 11, 1943). Consequences: The college's staff is reduced

Bill, scrupulously clean and an excellent carpenter, stops painting for once to build a bedroom in the middle of the loft: a platform bed, built-in storage, separate work areas at either end for him and Elaine. a platform bed, built-in storage, the central room of the large loft Consequences: the material preparation for the marriage

Hans and Sophie Scholl, members of the White Rose resistance, are guillotined by the Nazis after a sham trial for having denounced the war. Consequences: Their sister Inge founds the Geschwister-Scholl-Stiftung to build a school in the service of democracy
Albers writes the epigraph of the essay on the photographer and vision during his Black Mountain period.

The Addison buys the 1940 composition Bent Black (A), Albers himself lowering the price; Hayes does not reveal that Anne Peabody, who provides the funds, is the museum's registrar. Price lowered to 250 dollars; the donor's identity hidden from Albers Consequences: Albers's first entry into the Addison's collections
Stamos exhibits colorful, expressive landscapes.

The drama teacher Eric Bentley, trained at Oxford, translates Brecht's antifascist play The Private Life of the Master Race (1938), hoping that its liveliness will make it a powerful weapon in Allied propaganda. First reading in English at the college on February 16, 1944. Brecht's attacks on theatrical illusionism precede the spread of Artaud's similar ideas. first English reading: 1944-02-16

By the time he leaves Black Mountain in 1943, Wunsch has turned creative writing from a progressive experiment into artistic expression and provided the educational rationale ensuring its future at the college. Consequences: Creative writing continues after his departure.
Albers and Archer organize small photography exhibitions on campus, including Barbara Morgan's images of Martha Graham in 1943.
Enrolls briefly in pharmacology at the University of Texas at Austin before being drafted into the U.S. Navy.

Rauschenberg leaves Port Arthur in the fall of 1943 for the University of Texas; he begins pharmacy studies there, having given up at 13 the plan of a life in the ministry. the ministry given up at 13; he keeps going to church until after the war Consequences: expelled six months later for refusing to dissect a frog in anatomy class

A collection of patriotic and religious Resistance poetry is published in Paris under the Occupation, including texts by the former Surrealists Louis Aragon and Paul Éluard; Benjamin Péret will attack it violently in 1945. Consequences: Péret's pamphlet, “Le Déshonneur des poètes”

Spring 1943: Olson collaborates with the painter and photographer Ben Shahn, a former assistant of Diego Rivera, on a brochure for the Bataan campaign. a propaganda brochure Consequences: The first Olson-Shahn collaboration, before GLYPH

Thanks to the Harper prize money, the Rice family moves to Sarasota in the spring of 1943; there Rice writes slowly, in fits and starts, and tries fiction. Consequences: The start of his career as a short-story writer.

Driving past a field in Nevada, she spots a rich vein of green jasper and in two hours gathers enough for a whole mosaic. two hours of gathering; green jasper Consequences: the beginning of her familiarity with minerals found in nature

In a statement to the New York Times, Rothko and Gottlieb write: “There is no such thing as good painting about nothing” and assert that the subject is crucial. Text published in The New York Times. Consequences: An implicit manifesto on the content of American abstract painting.

She traces the numbers on aircraft dials with a pantograph, right hand, left hand, foot for the pressure; WQXR on the radio beside her; at midnight, everyone goes bowling Words: exactly like Charlie Chaplin in Modern Times; she reads all of Proust, in the Duke of Guermantes's drawing rooms Atmosphere: Mechanical rhythm and literary escape Stakes: Two years without a brush; she will come out of them in a totally different place

Having found the eight cows, they come back down over the stepping-stones of a creek bed, running at full speed, Dreier flying ahead like water skipping over the rocks. Atmosphere: the ecstasy of speed, a transcendent exhaustion, the morning sun turned to afternoon Stakes: a bodily knowledge and joy the witness will never be able to forget

Each day, the sophisticated visitor from the Kolisch Quartet sheds a layer — makeup, stockings, shoes, hairdo, scarves — before the eyes of the innocent girl from Milwaukee, until she is no more than a pin-up coming apart at the seams. Atmosphere: A silent comedy of sophistication undone by rural life. Stakes: A clash of worlds, the provincial girl's initiation.

Swamped with vegetables, Molly Gregory tries to sell them door to door in the village and is nearly arrested; she falls back on the open market in Asheville and gets pennies for them Atmosphere: Clownish, discouraging Stakes: The limits of heroic self-sufficiency

The ordinarily stiff and shy man gives one of the most eloquent speeches in the college's history: an eleventh year but a new college, an organic form, planning open to all, the oldest being the most conservative; he concludes with the wish for a year that is “orderly… in a beautiful sense” — at which the skeptics grumble Words: The wish for an orderly year — with orderly people in orderly rooms and studies, on an orderly campus — not in the military sense, but in the beautiful sense Atmosphere: Solemn, idealized, gently mocked by the skeptics Stakes: Redefining the community in the trough of the war

Alone with his copy of I Came Out of the Eighteenth Century, Holt scribbles denials in the margins (“never said it,” “not true”) next to the passages that offend him; reaching the sentence “Holt was determined to destroy me,” he writes “Until the last, I tried in every way to save him”; then, seized by a higher ambivalence: “Rice had a good side in not a few respects.” Words: Repeated marginal denials, then the final concession. Atmosphere: Anger turning into kindly melancholy; the book, an object of revenge, become a confidant. Stakes: The sworn enemy proves unable to hate completely.
Driving past a field, she spots a vein of green jasper; in two hours she gathers enough for a whole mosaic. Atmosphere: desert, the happy chance of discovery Stakes: art begins with a walk and a look

A text in the Bulletin asserts that music, as a world of inner order, can help develop the community for which we are all working — music as a model of community harmony. Bulletin 1, no. 3, February 1943

A brochure, “Learning and Living,” presenting the college's philosophy: a cosmopolitan community of students and teachers living together, an education founded on democratic cooperation, participation in community life, the discipline of the studio, the laboratory, and the work program on campus; it prepares citizens for the world at war and after the war. A rejection of the required curriculum, report cards, and the board of trustees; a preference for intensive work under guidance, discussion classes, and continuous contact with teachers rather than the syllabus and the weekly quiz. Open courses: a course in Field Work (?), a philosophy seminar, a series on music, a chorus; access to the college library and the record collection; five main types of work, including construction (mention of Kocher) Consequences: An institutional publicity document, useful for the college's official speeches
After nine months at the college, called to active duty in the air force. Consequences: The end of his stay at BMC.

An essay starting from a button among seashells to contrast the simplified order of manufactured objects with the variety of nature, criticize decoration as camouflage, and call for owning less and designing pure forms. essay dated “May, 1943”

With about 8,200 copies sold out of a printing of just over 10,000, the publisher withdraws the remaining stock. A year later, he refuses Rice's request for ten more personal copies. Holt, satisfied, does not go to court and annotates his personal copy. Holt's marginal notes: “never said it,” “not true,” “implication quite false,” “do not remember”; next to “Holt was determined to destroy me,” he writes “Until the last, I tried in every way to save him,” and finally “Rice had a good side in not a few respects”. Consequences: The book's commercial success is cut short.

Albers, in rumpled white trousers and a white shirt with rolled sleeves, rake in hand, directs the road crew: four girls are leveling a section. He explains the curve needed for drainage, smoothing the air with his hands as if polishing a marble bust. Powdery white dust in the nostrils, monstrous heat. From the Round House, piano arpeggios (probably Patsy Lynch, in the shade behind the glass doors). four girls; rakes and hoes; white dust; crushing heat; the glass doors of the Round House Consequences: when they had finished, that stretch of road was theirs

At the end of August 1943, the faculty, in the euphoria of the mica, decides to carry on regardless; summer pledges: $17,000; an expected enrollment of 55 students, 20-25% of them expected to be boys. $17,000 in pledges; 55 students hoped for Consequences: The new term goes ahead

By mid-October 1943, only one male student remains: Sam Brown, a polio victim; the others have left with the last Enlisted Reserve Corps unit; young women have left too — WACs, WAVES, munitions factories. Consequences: Not a single young American-born male teacher left in the community

Hansgirg announces to the Board of Fellows that his research on extracting magnesium from olivine (a mineral abundant in North Carolina) is progressing; he will found a small company holding the patents and offers the college a 20% interest as a gift. 20% interest Consequences: The gift will come to nothing: the company never materializes, the pilot operation destroyed by fire

The German word Werklehre is dropped because Germany is at war; its last official appearance is said to be the bulletin of December 1943. The course becomes “Basic Design” / “General Design,” but the students go on calling it Werklehre. Consequences: The course officially renamed.

Bill and Elaine serve as witnesses at the wedding of Ernestine Blumberg and Ibram Lassaw in 1944; then the couples go to a smorgasbord restaurant at $2 a person: a parade of incredible dishes, tiny portions, strangely compressed meat (black-hole meat); they try everything, since the price covers as much as they want. $2 a person, “black-hole” meat

In 1944, the first telephone is installed in the loft she shares with Bill; its constant ringing annoys him so much that he rips the instrument off the wall. telephone ripped off the wall Consequences: a contrast with her three telephones of 1962

In the summer of 1944, Charlot returns with his family, teaches a drawing course, and applies his fresco techniques (developed on his Mexican murals) to the concrete pillars of the new study building (Inspiración, Estudio). Frescoes on the concrete piers Consequences: The beginning of a lifelong friendship by letter with Josef

The following summer, Charlot and his family return to BMC; he teaches drawing there and applies the fresco techniques of his Mexican murals to the concrete columns of the new student building. Frescoes on load-bearing concrete columns Consequences: The beginning of a lasting friendship, kept up mainly by correspondence

After a concert of the 1944 summer session, Gretel invites the performers and some students; she opens the living room with Eva Heinitz, the star viola da gamba player, who screams and jumps onto the coffee table: a little green garter snake has come in with her. She comes down only when Gretel has removed the guest. a little green snake, a coffee table

In the spring of 1944, after tense meetings, the faculty, pushed by Dreier, had finally committed itself to admitting Black students; Dreier had worked hard with the Rosenwald Foundation. The conservatives say they must not go too fast, that they are not ready; the push stops and the direction reverses. Threats make themselves felt, possibly fires set on the grounds. Dreier is ordered to break off all negotiations with the foundation, which shatters trust in the commitment made; he is left alone. threats, possible fires on the college grounds Consequences: the question of Black students unresolved until the fall of 1945

The tone of this year has been one of growing dissonance: the beginning of a summer of terrifying tension. The witness discovers her personal responsibility for her thoughts and positions. Teachers take sides on opposing principles, at the cost of broken friendships and breaks with the college. Meanwhile the summer Music and Art Institutes are in full swing; the Kolisch Quartet rehearses a Schoenberg quartet whose faint sounds carry across the lake to the witness sitting at the loom in the silent basement of the Studies Building. a loom, a shuttle, sounds of music from the dining hall across the lake Consequences: an education of another order: “terra trema,” each person having to find firm ground

Albers had assigned Goulet to translate an abstract paper relief into a clay sculpture for the student building. De Creeft, seeing this, rejects the whole project and insists that she study direct carving in a material of real value; he thinks she is being used by the school, carrying out someone else's work instead of an original work. The panel will never be finished. a paper relief to translate into clay; a panel never finished Consequences: she takes his carving course; five months later she marries her sculpture teacher

Five months after taking de Creeft's carving course, she marries her sculpture teacher; thirty-eight years of marriage, fifteen solo exhibitions of carvings in wood and stone, rarely working in clay again. 38 years of marriage; 15 solo exhibitions Consequences: a whole career as a sculptor

A dazzling succession of celebrities teaches or lectures that summer. A chorus directed by Jalowetz rehearses all summer in the dining hall for a work by Schoenberg at the end of the session; the sound carried across the lake to the Studies Building. At least one concert a week; musicians heard rehearsing in between

She had her harpsichord shipped to North Carolina with the help of Theodore Dreier, who knew her from her earlier performances and as the teacher of Nathalie White Coleman, then a student. She played mainly solo Couperin, also solo Bach, and concertos under the direction of Jalowetz, whose authority as a conductor could bear comparison with Toscanini's, under whom she had often played with the NBC Symphony of the Air. When she was not there, Jalowetz led madrigals after dinner. Charlot made a small portrait of her, which she still owns.

One Saturday evening after dinner, the visiting sculptor José de Creeft improvises a bullfight: he is the matador, his future wife Lorrie Goulet the bull, and the author of the account the president who orders the fight to begin. the author wears a black cardboard top hat; no trophy (“ears”) awarded

The outside examiner Karl Veet, of Hamilton College, comes to put Jane Slater through two days of orals and three days of written examinations in art history. a demand for extreme erudition: knowing which Uccello is at Oxford

For the birthday of Dr. Hansgirg (who worked with Henry Kaiser, builder of the Liberty ships), many guests are invited to his cottage for a short concert — Bach, a trio sonata — on piano, cello, and violin, washed down with champagne with macerated peaches. peaches macerated for a week in 100-proof alcohol; after one or two, people were floating on the lawn; two mice come out and dance during the concert; his cream-colored Cadillac convertible nicknamed the “Cream Dream”

Marion calls her husband into the yard: under some dwarf pines grows a white hooded flower — an Oconee bell (Shortia galacifolia), a species named by André Michaux around 1790 and long impossible to find. Coron had searched in vain for two or three years on the cliffs of Toxaway Falls, fifty miles away; the plant had been transplanted from Highlands by Clark Foreman, a predecessor. 200-foot cliffs at Toxaway Falls; the flower found ten yards from the house Consequences: the author's greatest botanical joy

While hiking, Coron is stopped by an armed deputy sheriff in a slouch hat, who suspects him of having started a brush fire; he is put to work on the fire line. The mountain people sometimes set fires so as to be paid as firefighters.

In the middle of the night, a girl knocks at Coron's door: a fellow student is very ill. The ranger telephones the college; Molly Gregory, dean of women, drives fifteen miles of winding roads and arrives at 2 a.m. to bring the sick girl down. Back the next day: the culprit had smuggled in a bottle of “mountain dew” and drunk without restraint. Mount Mitchell, the highest peak in the East, 15 miles from the college; arrival at 2 a.m.
On a hike with former GIs in steep country, the group is arrested for illegal fishing in a federal preserve and hauled one Sunday morning before a justice of the peace, who fines them.

Coming out of Meadows Inn after a heavy rain, Coron notices in the washed gravel a small, perfectly worked arrowhead; he starts looking for them, especially in the sloping cornfield, and finds many, a number of them unfinished — a sign, in his view, of an age-old workshop on Cherokee hunting grounds. Consequences: sets off Coron's vocation as a historian of the Southern Indians: research at the Asheville Public Library, three books, articles, a post at Roosevelt University, a fellowship at the Newberry Library

After dinner, during a summer thunderstorm, a round table on dance as an art form; de Mille, a few years after choreographing Oklahoma!, asserts with a pointed forefinger that it was the Church that banned dance from worship — at that very moment a deafening clap of thunder rolls: a shiver, a collective gasp, then general helpless laughter led by de Mille. a summer heat storm after supper; a raised forefinger to punctuate the conviction

Sadoff and Cohen play four hands on the dining hall's two grand pianos for an evening of music from Carmen; student singers sing to their accompaniment; the Habanera, with its rubatos and excesses of tempo, is a triumph.

Jean Charlot directs the making of frescoes on the broad cement piers supporting the long wing of the Studies Building that juts out from the hillside; the work is done in the cool shade, mixing and shoveling cement.

Charlot directs the making of frescoes on one of the broad cement piers supporting the wing of the Studies Building that juts out from the hill. Work in the cool shade: mixing and shoveling cement, tracings of diagrams on brown paper transferred to the wall section by section as it dries. brown paper for the tracings, fresh mortar, pigments Consequences: the beginning of Woldin's fascination with wet mortar, pigments, and the mystery of binding

Cutting cornstalks with machetes, piling them up, chopping them, and blowing them into the top of the silo; a task in which everyone was in principle to take part. The rhythm of the machetes and the energy of the group made physical work in the sun almost effortless. machetes, a chopper, a silo, enormous dust, a blazing sun, files of ants Consequences: confirms the belief inherited at the college: shared manual work balances solitary thought and artistic effort

Woldin walks confidently into the little town, sure she will find a library; a passerby on the dusty road that serves as the main street tells her it is upstairs over the jail and opens only now and then. a dusty main road, the library over the jail

On carefree hikes, the students come upon chain gangs: men in leg irons, chained together or dragging heavy iron balls, in striped uniforms, moving slowly under the rifles of guards with their fingers on the trigger, barrels pushed close to the prisoners' faces. leg irons, iron balls, striped uniforms, rifles, files of ants, dusty roads Consequences: a spectacle of humiliation hard to absorb; questions set aside, little or no discussion at the college during the summer of 1944, the artistic mission absorbing everything

She comes from Westport (Connecticut), despite her family's preference for an Ivy League school, with average grades and an ardent idealism. Sammy Brown, a student, had come to describe life at BMC to her worried family (“radical kid”). Mac Wood, teacher of carpentry and small-house design, picks her up at the station in the college truck. the college truck, the railroad station

An immediate identity entrusted to Janet: coordinator of the furnace crew, of the Studies Building stoker, and of the formidable high-pressure boiler under the dining hall, which had to be fed without letting the pressure rise too dangerously. Dee Carr, her study companion, is her assistant, helped by Lorna Pearson and Earlene Wight. Ben Sneed, the handyman, drunk and asleep in the coal bin, delights in telling stories of boiler explosions while they anxiously watch the pressure gauge. the coal bin, the pressure gauge, coal, high pressure Consequences: without this identity, she would have drifted seriously at BMC

Foreman having become president of the SCHW, its executive committee sits for several days at the college; two long informal meetings with the community on the problems of democracy; the leaders unanimously declare themselves in favor of admitting Black students Consequences: The question crystallizes the resentments of the “old-timers” against the new staff

Months of meetings, from secret caucuses to marathon sessions of the whole community; personal antagonisms and side issues (communism, laxity toward students, the value of the work program) fragment the community into shifting camps where no one any longer knows why X is shouting at Y At least one student and the assistant treasurer resign under the threat of what was called a black tide Consequences: The community split of 1944
Lawyer friends look into it: no North Carolina law requires segregation in higher education (unlike the schools through the 12th grade) Consequences: The opposition's legal argument falls

Foreman has lawyer friends check the North Carolina statutes: no law requires segregation in higher education (unlike the schools through the twelfth grade). Legal segregation required only up to and including the 12th grade. Consequences: Legally, nothing prevents admitting Black students; the opposition changes its argument.

Thirty-eight students out of fifty sign a petition in favor of admitting more than one Black student. 38 signatures out of 50 students. Consequences: The faculty vote (a single Black member) reveals that the students carry weight only on trivial questions or when their opinion coincides with the teachers'.

To prove that the South is not ready, Wunsch solicits the opinion of Black educators close to the college; he gets the answers he was looking for. Letters from Hurston and Rubye Lipsey. Consequences: Strengthens the camp of caution.
